name: Phentermine
summary: A prescription appetite suppressant related to amphetamine, approved for short-term use alongside a weight-loss program; a Schedule IV controlled substance.
what_it_is: Phentermine, sold under brand names including Adipex-P, is a prescription appetite suppressant. Its label describes it as a sympathomimetic amine, chemically and pharmacologically related to amphetamine. It is approved only for short-term use (a few weeks) as an add-on to a weight-reduction program in people with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or more, or 27 or more with other risk factors.

evidence.why: It is FDA-approved for short-term weight loss; evidence on longer use comes mainly from observational health-record studies, not long-term randomized trials.

status_us.label: FDA-approved for short-term weight loss; Schedule IV
status_us.note: Adipex-P is approved only as a short-term (a few weeks) add-on in a weight-reduction program for people with a BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with other risk factors. It is a Schedule IV controlled substance, and longer-term use is off-label.

benefits.claim: Short-term weight loss as an add-on to a weight-reduction program in people with a BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with other risk factors (approved use)

Off-label longer use (the label approves only short-term use, a few weeks): among 13,972 adults in US health systems, those who took it continuously for more than a year lost 7.4% more of their body weight at 2 years than short-term users; this kind of study cannot prove cause, and weight came back after stopping
Slightly lower systolic blood pressure at 2 years in longer-term (off-label) users in that study, which the authors linked to greater weight loss

risks.risk: Heart and blood pressure: raised blood pressure, palpitations, a fast heart rate and ischemic events such as heart attacks are listed side effects; the label rules it out in people with a history of heart disease and urges caution even with mild high blood pressure; one health-record study of longer use found no significant rise in heart attacks, strokes or deaths, but only 41 occurred, too few to rule out harm

Primary pulmonary hypertension, a rare and frequently fatal lung-artery disease, and heart valve disease; valve disease has been reported rarely with phentermine alone, and new, unexplained shortness of breath needs prompt medical review
Overstimulation, restlessness, insomnia, dizziness and tremor; psychosis has also been reported
Misuse and dependence: it is related to amphetamine and is a Schedule IV controlled substance; stopping after long, high-dose use can cause extreme tiredness and depression
The appetite effect can wear off as tolerance develops
It can impair driving and other hazardous tasks, and alcohol may cause adverse reactions

avoid_if: History of heart disease, including coronary artery disease, stroke, irregular heart rhythm, heart failure or uncontrolled high blood pressure (contraindicated)
Taking an MAO inhibitor now or within the past 14 days (contraindicated)
Overactive thyroid, glaucoma, agitated states or a history of drug misuse (contraindicated)
Athletes in tested sports (WADA bans phentermine in competition)
interactions: MAO inhibitors: risk of a dangerous rise in blood pressure (hypertensive crisis); not to be used together or within 14 days
Other weight-loss drugs, and serotonergic drugs such as SSRI antidepressants: the label says combining them is not recommended
Insulin and other diabetes medicines: requirements may change, which the prescriber manages
Adrenergic neuron-blocking blood pressure drugs: their effect may be reduced

during: Blood glucose in people with diabetes, whose medicine needs may change
labs.why: The label focuses on heart and blood-pressure history rather than blood tests; people with diabetes may need closer glucose checks.

studies.title: Safety and Effectiveness of Longer-Term Phentermine Use: Clinical Outcomes from an Electronic Health Record Cohort
studies.people: 13,972 adults aged 18 to 64 in US integrated health systems
studies.finding: Compared with short-term use, more than a year of continuous use was linked with 7.4% more weight loss at 2 years and no significant difference in heart events or death (41 events in total). The design was observational, and the authors called for randomized trials.

studies.title: ADIPEX-P (phentermine hydrochloride): prescribing information
studies.people: People with a BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with other risk factors
studies.finding: Approved for short-term use only; ruled out with heart disease, MAO inhibitors, overactive thyroid, glaucoma, agitated states, a history of drug misuse, pregnancy and nursing.

ask_your_clinician: Are my heart and blood pressure healthy enough for phentermine?
How long would I take it, and what is the plan for keeping weight off afterward?
Would a medicine approved for long-term weight management suit me better?

sources.title: Safety and Effectiveness of Longer-Term Phentermine Use: Clinical Outcomes from an Electronic Health Record Cohort
sources.publisher: Obesity (copy hosted by the Chilean Society of Obesity)

notes_for_editor: Label is Adipex-P (revised March 2024, Drugs.com copy); the Lomaira label was not opened. The label's adverse-reaction section, as read, lists only body systems without rates, so no side-effect frequencies are given. The label's pulmonary hypertension warning was only partly read (the valve-disease line about phentermine alone was read in full). The Lewis cohort is observational, the long-term continuous group was small (144), and the referent group may include people who stopped because it did not work; it did not assess anxiety, sleep problems or addiction. The PDF is a copy on the Chilean Society of Obesity's site (the URL contains a non-ASCII hyphen). The phentermine-topiramate combination product (Qsymia) was not researched.
